Sofía was 9 years old at her Vineland-3 interview on 10/05/2026. During the home interview that day, her mother, Carmen Inventada, described Sofía as a strong reader who remembers train schedules, enjoys drawing maps, helps feed the family dog and is affectionate with her maternal grandmother. Carmen reported that Sofía lives with her, her 6-year-old brother Diego and their 72-year-old maternal grandmother, who cares for the children from 3:00 to 5:30 p.m. while Carmen works. According to Carmen, Sofía’s father lives in another state and has no regular contact. The BCBA conducted the interview with Carmen in English; Carmen reported that the grandmother speaks only Spanish and is willing to learn strategies to use with Sofía.

Carmen reported that Sofía was born at 39 weeks without complications, met early milestones on time and spoke in sentences by age 2. According to Carmen, teachers first raised concerns in kindergarten because Sofía had outbursts and played alone. Carmen reported that 6 months of school counseling in 2024 “did not change anything” and that Sofía has never received ABA.

According to the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation (CDE), Ramón Ejemplar, M.D., Sofía’s pediatrician and primary care physician, referred her because of aggression at home and school, explosive outbursts, leaving the classroom, school refusal and lack of friendships. Marta Supuesta, Ph.D., a Florida-licensed psychologist, evaluated Sofía on 07/15/2026 and 07/22/2026. In the report signed 07/30/2026, Dr. Supuesta diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder (F84.0), without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language, and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation (F90.2). [MISSING: DSM-5 autism support level, not specified in the available CDE notes.] During her 2-hour summer program observation on 07/22/2026, Dr. Supuesta observed that Sofía talked to an adult about train schedules for 15 minutes without checking the adult’s interest, shoved a peer who sat in her preferred seat and left the group activity twice. Dr. Supuesta recommended ABA at home and in the community for aggression, emotional regulation, flexibility and social skills, with parent training. She also recommended continued school speech-language services, a social skills group, medication management and coordination with the school team. According to the CDE notes, Dr. Ejemplar signed the physician’s order for behavior analysis on 08/04/2026.

The CDE identified Iván Hipotético, M.D., Sofía’s psychiatrist, as the prescriber of methylphenidate extended release, 18 mg every morning, started in March 2026. Carmen confirmed the dose during the parent interview and reported better focus in the morning but worse outbursts in the afternoon than before medication began. She reported psychiatry follow-up every 6 weeks. In the caregiver FBA interview, Carmen identified poor sleep and changes in routine as circumstances in which Sofía has more difficulty.

According to Carmen, Sofía attends 4th grade at Ejemplo Elementary School from 8:30 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in a general education classroom with ESE support. Her IEP, in effect from 04/17/2026 to 04/16/2027, documents grade-level reading and strong vocabulary. Although Sofía uses complete sentences, the IEP describes difficulty taking conversational turns and understanding nonliteral language. In math, the IEP places her about 1 year below grade level and notes that she does not finish independent work. The IEP provides 300 minutes per week of support facilitation in general education, 60 minutes per week of school speech-language therapy for pragmatic language and 30 minutes per week of school counseling. It also provides a visual schedule, advance notice of transitions and a break card. The IEP documents that Sofía leaves the classroom without permission 2 to 4 times per week, usually during writing or group work, and has physical altercations with peers about 2 times per week, mostly at lunch and recess. The IEP does not include behavior analysis services. According to the BCBA’s 10/28/2026 follow-up notes, the school-based FBA requested on 04/17/2026 was still pending, and Carmen signed releases for the school and psychiatrist.

At home, Carmen identified preventing injury to Diego as her first priority. She reported that Sofía hits, kicks or pushes him several times a day, often over the tablet or TV remote, and that he had a bruise on his upper arm the week before the interview. During the 10/07/2026 home observation, the BCBA saw Sofía push Diego to the floor and kick his leg after he picked up her train book. Carmen also reported that Sofía bites her hand or wrist when frustrated. According to Carmen, on 09/14/2026 Sofía struck her head against the bedroom wall during an outburst and sustained a cut above her eyebrow that was closed with skin glue at urgent care; the BCBA did not have the urgent care record. Beyond safety, Carmen wants Sofía to calm down without breaking things, go to school without a fight, make a friend and shower independently. During the 10/14/2026 evening observation, the BCBA recorded 14 verbal prompts over 38 minutes before Sofía entered the shower; she did not wash her hair.

Changes in routine are a particular concern for the family. During the 10/28/2026 follow-up call, Carmen recalled that school refusal began around the time the bus route changed in early September, when a new driver began picking Sofía up 15 minutes earlier. Carmen reported that the grandmother would be away from 12/15/2026 to 01/20/2027. In a phone call with the BCBA on 11/20/2026, Carmen confirmed that the YMCA after-school program at Ejemplo Elementary School had accepted Sofía beginning 12/15/2026 and that she had given the program a copy of Sofía’s IEP accommodations. Carmen also reported a planned move to another school zone in March 2027 that would require a school change. She expressed concern about preparing Sofía for the move because even a change in the route home can lead to screaming and refusal to get out of the car.

To assess Sofía’s need for ABA, Daniela Muestra, M.S., BCBA, reviewed the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation (CDE) completed by Marta Supuesta, Ph.D., a Florida-licensed psychologist, on 07/15/2026 and 07/22/2026 and signed 07/30/2026, and the 04/17/2026 IEP from Ejemplo Elementary School, including the teacher’s account of behavior in class. On 10/05/2026, the BCBA interviewed Sofía’s mother, Carmen Inventada, at home and administered the Vineland-3 Comprehensive Parent/Caregiver Interview Form, BASC-3 Parenting Relationship Questionnaire (PRQ), Child/Adolescent form, Functional Analysis Screening Tool (FAST), Motivation Assessment Scale (MAS) and caregiver FBA interview with Carmen as respondent. The BCBA directly observed homework at home on 10/07/2026, a public library and neighborhood park outing on 10/10/2026, and dinner, shower and bedtime routines at home on 10/14/2026. Carmen provided follow-up information by phone on 10/28/2026 and 11/20/2026. Dr. Supuesta diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder (F84.0), without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language, and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation (F90.2). [MISSING: DSM-5 autism support level, not specified in the available CDE notes.] Together, the findings identify limitations in communication, daily living skills, socialization and social participation, safety during transitions, and behavioral regulation.

On the Vineland-3, Carmen’s responses yielded an Adaptive Behavior Composite standard score of 74 (4th percentile, Moderately Low), indicating that Sofía manages everyday demands less independently than most children her age. Communication was 81 (10th percentile, Moderately Low); Expressive skills were Adequate (v-scale 13), but Receptive and Written skills were Moderately Low (12 and 11). Daily Living Skills was 72 (3rd percentile, Moderately Low), with greater difficulty in Community (8, Low) and Domestic skills (9, Low) than in Personal skills (10, Moderately Low). Socialization was 66 (1st percentile, Low); Coping (5), Interpersonal Relationships (7) and Play and Leisure (9) were all Low, with managing frustration and change a particular difficulty. Motor Skills was a relative strength at 88 (21st percentile, Adequate); Sofía’s ability to move independently does not mean she can navigate a street safely. On the Maladaptive Behavior domain, where higher scores indicate more difficulty, Internalizing was Elevated (v-scale 19), and Externalizing and the Maladaptive Behavior Index were both Clinically Significant (22 each). Carmen rated hitting, kicking or pushing others, damaging property, threatening others and refusing school as occurring often. These ratings describe the extent of the concerns; the behavior-specific observations and interviews below inform the hypotheses about function.

Although the IEP documents complete sentences, strong vocabulary and grade-level reading, it also describes difficulty taking conversational turns and understanding nonliteral language. Dr. Supuesta documented that Sofía does not ask questions back or repair misunderstandings and misreads teasing as aggression. Carmen described long stretches of talk about trains. At home on 10/07/2026, the BCBA listened as Sofía discussed train schedules for 11 minutes without responding to 2 attempts to change the topic. Her difficulty is not a lack of words but adjusting what she says in response to another person. ABA will use modeling, practice and feedback in everyday conversations to teach Sofía to pause, respond to a partner’s comment and ask for clarification. Practice with family and community partners will complement, rather than replace, the pragmatic language therapy provided under her IEP.

For daily living, Carmen reported that Sofía can dress herself and helps feed the dog but does not wash her hair independently and cannot order food or pay in a store. During the 10/14/2026 home observation, the BCBA recorded 14 verbal prompts over 38 minutes before Sofía entered the shower; she did not wash her hair. The Personal and Community scores thus reflect practical limits: a caregiver must repeatedly interrupt the evening routine to prompt hygiene, and Sofía cannot complete an everyday purchase on her own. ABA will break showering and hair washing into observable steps, reinforce steps completed independently and fade prompts. Guided practice ordering and paying will address the separate skills Sofía needs when a cashier speaks to her.

The Low Socialization score is reflected in missed opportunities to join peers even when they initiate contact. Carmen reported that Sofía has no friends at school or in the neighborhood. During the 2-hour summer program observation on 07/22/2026, Dr. Supuesta observed Sofía playing alone during free time and shoving a peer who sat in her preferred seat. At the park on 10/10/2026, the BCBA observed 2 girls invite Sofía to play tag. She recited the bus schedule instead; the girls walked away, and she played alone. ABA will teach Sofía to recognize an invitation, answer it and join a shared activity. Practice during community play will extend the IEP’s structured conversational turn-taking goal to situations in which no adult directs the exchange.

For leaving the area and school refusal, the BCBA recorded 1 community episode: on the way to the park, Sofía pulled her wrist free of Carmen’s hand and ran across the street without looking. There were no cars at that moment, but the crossing presented an immediate injury risk. At school, the IEP documents leaving class without permission 2 to 4 times per week, usually during writing or group work; Dr. Supuesta directly observed Sofía leave the group twice and be found in the hallway. The BCBA did not observe at school because district approval was pending. Carmen reported school refusal on 6 of 20 school days in October [CHECK: the 10/05/2026 interview notes give this October count; verify the attendance period with Carmen or school records]. Carmen reported that she arrived late to work or the grandmother kept Sofía home on those days. The MAS escape score of 5.0 on a 0-to-6 scale and the school task patterns support hypothesized escape from academic and social demands; the street crossing establishes danger, not its function. ABA will teach Sofía to stop, look and wait before crossing with an adult, rehearse changes to the school-morning routine and practice requesting a break rather than leaving, consistent with her IEP break card.

Across 6 hours of observation, the BCBA recorded 6 episodes of physical aggression, including pushing Diego to the floor and kicking him after he picked up Sofía’s train book. Carmen reported a bruise on Diego’s upper arm, and the IEP documents peer altercations about 2 times per week. For physical aggression, Carmen’s FAST escape endorsements (4 of 4) and MAS scores (escape 4.5, tangible 3.8) support escape from demands as the primary hypothesis and access to preferred items as secondary. The BCBA also recorded 6 verbal outbursts lasting 6 to 15 minutes (mean 9.7 minutes) and 3 episodes of property destruction. On 10/07/2026, Sofía tore her math worksheet and screamed for 12 minutes; her grandmother gave her the tablet, and neither homework attempt was completed. The IEP documents almost daily verbal outbursts and a chair thrown during a transition to writing on 03/12/2026, after which the class was evacuated for about 25 minutes. FAST escape endorsements of 4 of 4 for each behavior support hypothesized escape from demands and transitions for verbal outbursts and escape from demands for property destruction. The BCBA recorded 3 episodes of hand biting (self-injury), including 2 bites that left red marks during a second homework attempt. FAST endorsements suggest escape as primary (3 of 4) and automatic sensory stimulation as secondary (2 of 4). Separately, Carmen reported that head banging on 09/14/2026 caused a cut requiring skin glue at urgent care; the record was unavailable. To reduce injury and preserve participation, ABA will teach and differentially reinforce requesting help, a break or a turn with an item, using a calming strategy and returning to an interrupted task.

These findings support the medical necessity of ABA at home and in the community, where the BCBA directly observed injury risk, dependence during hygiene and difficulty sustaining peer interaction. Treatment will pair replacement-skill practice in those routines with school coordination so that break requests and transition cues are consistent without duplicating school instruction, counseling or speech-language therapy. On the BASC-3 PRQ, Carmen’s ratings of Attachment and Involvement were Average, while Discipline Practices (T-score 36), Parenting Confidence (34), Satisfaction with School (31) and Relational Frustration (68) were At-Risk. Carmen described feeling “exhausted and judged,” avoiding outings and dropping homework “to keep the peace.” Caregiver training will use rehearsal and feedback to help Carmen and the Spanish-speaking grandmother respond consistently to break requests, reinforce safe behavior and resume routines after a break, with training accessible in Spanish for the grandmother. The BCBA will measure target behavior frequency, outburst duration, independent requests, successful transitions, safe crossings and self-care steps completed without prompts. At reassessment, the Vineland-3 and BASC-3 PRQ will complement those direct measures by assessing broader changes in Sofía’s independence and Carmen’s experience managing daily routines.

The BCBA will teach each replacement behavior with a consistent cue (discriminative stimulus) and then keep that cue the same as the person, activity or setting changes. For example, Sofía’s IEP specifies a visual cue for using her break card during class. At home, Sofía will practice using the card in response to the same cue during homework with her mother, Carmen, and her maternal grandmother, then returning to the unfinished task after the break. The BCBA will provide coaching in Spanish for the grandmother and coordinate with Sofía’s teacher at Ejemplo Elementary School so that practice at home supports the classroom goal. On 11/20/2026, Carmen confirmed that she had shared the IEP accommodations with the YMCA after-school program; the BCBA will check which cues staff plan to use rather than assume the break card is in use there. For social practice, Sofía will take conversational turns on a topic chosen by her brother Diego at home and practice responding to peers’ invitations at the neighborhood park. During outings to the public library and park, Sofía will practice stopping, looking and waiting with an adult before crossing. As Sofía becomes more proficient, the BCBA will adjust the prompt hierarchy, giving her an opportunity to respond to the cue before adding a reminder and maintaining adult supervision at street crossings.

The BCBA will conduct weekly probes of each mastered skill to check whether Sofía continues to perform it in the routine where she needs it. For example, the BCBA will record whether Sofía uses her break card and returns to homework without an additional reminder, which showering and hair-washing steps she completes without verbal prompts, and whether she stops, looks and waits at the curb with an adult. For each mastered skill, the BCBA will move from continuous reinforcement of independent responses to intermittent reinforcement and fade teaching prompts while keeping the routine cue in place. If weekly probes show a decline from the mastered level, the BCBA will reinstate the previous reinforcement schedule and the prompts that were removed. Once Sofía regains that level, the BCBA will thin reinforcement and fade those prompts again.

Physical aggression places Sofía’s 6-year-old brother Diego at risk of repeated injury. During the 10/05/2026 interview, her mother, Carmen Inventada, reported that Sofía hits, kicks or pushes Diego several times a day, often over the tablet or TV remote, and that he had a bruise on his upper arm the week before the interview. Across 6 hours of home and community observation, the BCBA recorded 6 episodes of physical aggression. On 10/07/2026, the BCBA saw Sofía push Diego to the floor and kick his leg after he picked up her train book; he cried, but there was no visible injury. At the park on 10/10/2026, the BCBA saw Sofía push Diego off a swing. At home on 10/14/2026, when dinner was 10 minutes later than usual, the BCBA saw Sofía hit Carmen’s arm twice. At school, the 04/17/2026 IEP documents pushing or kicking peers about 2 times per week, mostly at lunch and recess. Carmen reported a 1-day suspension in May 2026 after Sofía kicked a classmate. During the summer program observation on 07/22/2026, Dr. Marta Supuesta saw Sofía shove a peer who sat in her preferred seat.

Verbal outbursts are of particular concern when Sofía threatens someone within reach. The BCBA recorded 6 outbursts in 6 hours, lasting 6 to 15 minutes (mean 9.7 minutes), including a 15-minute bedtime episode during which Sofía said, “I’ll run away.” Carmen reported outbursts nearly every day after school and at bedtime, sometimes lasting half an hour; the IEP describes almost daily outbursts when tasks change or Sofía loses a game. On 10/28/2026, Carmen described an August incident in which Sofía picked up a butter knife during an argument with Diego and told him, “I’ll kill you.” According to Carmen, Sofía put the knife down when her grandmother asked, and no one was hurt. Carmen reported that kitchen knives have since been stored in a high cabinet and that there are no firearms in the home. She said that during outbursts she or the grandmother sends Diego to his room, moves breakable objects out of reach and waits for Sofía to become quiet.

Property destruction also puts people nearby at risk when Sofía throws or kicks objects. The BCBA recorded 3 episodes in 6 hours, all at home. During homework on 10/07/2026, Sofía tore her worksheet and threw her pencil case across the room; during the delayed dinner on 10/14/2026, she kicked a chair over. Carmen reported that Sofía tears homework about half the time it is assigned, broke the TV remote on 10/01/2026 and tore a school library book in September. At school, the teacher’s account in the IEP documents that Sofía threw a chair on 03/12/2026 when asked to move from the computer to a writing assignment. The class was evacuated to the hallway while Sofía calmed down, which took about 25 minutes.

For hand biting (self-injury), the BCBA recorded 3 episodes in 6 hours: Sofía bit the back of her left hand twice during a second homework attempt on 10/07/2026, leaving red marks without breaking the skin, and bit her right wrist once when the tablet was removed at bedtime on 10/14/2026. Separately from the hand-biting baseline, Carmen reported that on 09/14/2026 Sofía struck her head against the bedroom wall during an outburst. According to Carmen, the grandmother took Sofía to urgent care for a cut above her eyebrow that was cleaned and closed with skin glue. The BCBA did not have the urgent care record. At follow-up on 10/28/2026, Carmen reported no subsequent injuries requiring medical care.

For leaving the area and school refusal, the most immediate danger the BCBA observed was at a street crossing. On the way to the park on 10/10/2026, Sofía pulled her wrist free of Carmen’s hand and ran across the street without looking. The BCBA recorded 1 such episode; no cars were present at that moment. Carmen reported that Sofía runs across streets without looking when excited and that she holds Sofía’s wrist in parking lots. At school, the IEP documents that Sofía leaves the classroom without permission 2 to 4 times per week, usually during writing or group work, and is found in the hallway or media center. Dr. Supuesta observed Sofía leave the group twice during the 2-hour summer program observation; she was found in the hallway. The BCBA did not observe at school because district approval was pending. According to Carmen, on those mornings she arrived late to work or Sofía stayed home with her grandmother.
